newsitem.title: USA: Rapid increase seen in alternative fueled vehicles.
newsitem.headline: Rapid increase seen in alternative fueled vehicles.

text.p: Vehicles fueled by alcohol, electricity and natural gas should increase rapidly from now until 2015, according to the U.S. Department of Energy's Energy Information Administration (EIA).

In an address at the National Conference on Ethanol Policy and Marketing here, EIA Administrator Jay Hakes said the EIA estimates more than 1.6 million alternative fueled vehicles will be sold in 2015 versus fewer than 50,000 in 1995.
Of that total, "ethanol vehicle sales should reach 190,000 by 2015," Hakes said. "Two-thirds of these (ethanol) vehicles are expected to be capable of using either gasoline or ethanol."

Hakes said the estimates are based on the assumption Washington will extend the federal tax incentive for ethanol fuels beyond its scheduled expiration in 2000. Ethanol blenders get 5.4 cents of the 18.3 cents per gallon federal gasoline tax paid by motorists when they buy fuel made with ethanol.
"We just have assumed, since it has been extended in the past, it will be extended in the future," he said.
The conference, which runs through Wednesday, is sponsored by the Renewable Fuels Association. Ethanol is a fuel additive made from corn.

Ford Motor Co builds Taurus cars that run on fuels containing 85 percent ethanol. It also builds a methanol-fueled Taurus, and has orders for an electric-powered Ranger pickup it will begin building in December, said Rachel Dickerson, a group leader in Ford's Alternative Fuel Vehicle unit.
Dickerson, who spoke at the conference, told Reuters that Ford is committed to making alternative-fueled vehicles.
"We are seeing a great number of states buying (ethanol-fueled cars)," she said.
In 1997, Ford has the capacity to build 12,000 cars fueled by methanol or ethanol, she said.

Gerald Barnes, a panelist at the conference and manager of General Motors Corp's Clean Fuels and Heavy Duty Activities, said unacceptable wear on engine parts prompted GM to delay its ethanol program.
